replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word **"unbelievable"** into an LLM, the model doesn't see a word at all.

It sees *three chunks*: `un` / `believ` / `able`.

That's because LLMs don't read language the way you do — they break everything into **tokens** first.

---

A token is a fragment of text — sometimes a whole word, sometimes part of one, sometimes just punctuation.

GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 possible tokens.

[KEY]Every word you type gets sliced into tokens, and each token gets converted into a number before the model does anything else.[/KEY]

[EX]The sentence "I went to the bank" might tokenize as: `I` / ` went` / ` to` / ` the` / ` bank` — five tokens, five numbers. The model has no idea yet whether "bank" means a riverbank or a financial institution. That ambiguity is a real problem it has to solve later.[/EX]

---

Here's the key thing about those numbers: they're not random IDs.

Each token gets mapped into a high-dimensional space — hundreds or thousands of coordinates — where *meaning* is encoded by position.

Tokens that appear in similar contexts end up close together in that space. "Doctor" and "physician" land near each other. "Bank" (financial) and "bank" (river) actually land in *different* neighborhoods depending on context.

---

[Q]
What does a tokenizer actually hand to the rest of the model?
A) The original words, spell-checked and cleaned up
B) A list of numbers representing text fragments
C) A lookup table of dictionary definitions
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) A list of numbers representing text fragments
replies.raw:
Exactly right — the tokenizer's whole job is to hand off numbers, not words.

That's what makes the next step possible.

---

Once the model has those numbers, it needs to figure out which tokens *matter* for understanding each other.

This is where the **attention mechanism** comes in.

For every token in your prompt, attention asks: "Which other tokens should I be paying attention to right now?"

[KEY]Attention lets the model weigh how relevant every other token is to the one it's currently processing — so context shapes meaning.[/KEY]

[EX]In "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired," attention figures out that "it" refers to "animal" — not "street." It does this by learning which token relationships matter, across the whole sentence at once.[/EX]

---

This is how "bank" stops being ambiguous.

If nearby tokens include "river" and "fishing," attention pulls those into focus and the model treats "bank" as a riverbank.

If nearby tokens include "loan" and "interest," it lands somewhere completely different.

---

[Q]
What problem does the attention mechanism mainly solve?
A) It checks the model's output for spelling errors
B) It decides which tokens in the prompt are relevant to each other
C) It speeds up tokenization so the model runs faster
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: can we keep going with the lesson
replies.raw:
Picked B again — and that's the right call.

Attention is what lets the model hold the whole sentence in mind at once, rather than reading left to right like a human does.

---

Now here's where it all comes together: **next-token prediction**.

After tokenization and attention, the model does one thing — it predicts what token should come next.

It doesn't "think up" an answer. It assigns a probability to every token in its 100,000-token vocabulary and picks from the top candidates.

[KEY]Every word in an AI's response is chosen one token at a time, by asking "given everything so far, what comes next?"[/KEY]

[EX]Finish this: "The cat sat on the ___." The model assigns high probability to "mat," "floor," "couch" — and near-zero probability to "democracy" or "seventeen." It's not retrieving a fact; it's completing a pattern.[/EX]

---

This is also why AI can sound confident and be completely wrong.

The model is optimizing for *plausible-sounding* next tokens — not for *true* ones.

Fluency and accuracy are two different things, and next-token prediction only guarantees the first.

---

Now here's where it gets interesting: knowing a token's number isn't enough. The model also needs to know what that token *means* in context.

That's where **embedding** and the **attention mechanism** come in — but let's focus on where this whole process is heading: **next-token prediction**.

After your prompt is tokenized, the model does one job, over and over: look at all the tokens so far and predict the single most likely *next* token.

Then it adds that token to the sequence and predicts the next one. Then the next. That's the entire output — one token at a time, each prediction feeding into the next.

[EX]Give the model "The cat sat on the ___" and it will assign high probability to tokens like "mat," "floor," "couch" — and very low probability to "democracy" or "seventeen." It's not retrieving a stored answer. It's calculating which token fits best, statistically, given everything before it.[/EX]

[KEY]An LLM generates responses by predicting one token at a time — not by looking up answers.[/KEY]

This is a crucial distinction from a search engine, which fetches existing pages. The model is *generating*, not retrieving.

[Q]
How does an LLM produce its response?
A) It predicts one token at a time based on what came before
B) It retrieves the closest sentence from its training data
C) It searches the internet for the best matching answer
ANS: A
[/Q]

Here's a wild fact to kick us off:

The sentence "I went to the bank" contains a word that could mean a riverbank or a financial institution — and a computer reading it one character at a time has *no idea* which one you mean.

That's exactly the problem that **tokenization** was invented to solve.

---

When you type a prompt, the very first thing an LLM does is chop your text into *tokens* — chunks that are roughly word-sized, but not exactly.

"Unbelievable" might become three tokens: `Un`, `believ`, `able`. A single emoji might be one token. A space before a word often gets attached to it as its own token.

---

Here's why this matters: the model never actually reads letters or words. It reads *numbers*.

Every token gets converted to a number (or ID), and that number is the model's way of saying "this chunk of text." GPT-4 has a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 possible tokens — so every word or word-piece you type maps to one of those 100,000 slots.

---

Think of it like a massive lookup table: your sentence goes in as human text, and what the model actually processes is a list of integers.

"The cat sat" might become `[464, 3797, 3332]` — three numbers in a row, ready for the next stage.

Here's a wild fact to kick us off:

The word "bank" — as in riverbank or as in Chase Bank — is the **same token** to an LLM. The model has no idea which meaning you intend until it processes the surrounding words. That ambiguity is baked into the very first step.

---

So what is a token, exactly?

When you type a prompt, the LLM doesn't read letters or words the way you do. It first chops your text into **tokens** — chunks that are roughly syllables or short words — and converts each one into a number.

"Unbelievable" might become three tokens: `Un` / `believ` / `able`. A space before a word often counts as part of the token. GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of around 100,000 possible tokens.

[EX]Type "I went to the bank to fish." The tokenizer splits it, maps each chunk to a number (say, token #4921 for "bank"), and hands a list of numbers to the rest of the model. At this stage, "bank" is just a number — no meaning attached yet.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization turns your text into a sequence of numbers before the model does any "thinking."[/KEY]

---

What does a tokenizer actually convert your words into?
A) A dictionary definition of each word

replies.raw:
Exactly right — tokenization is step zero, turning your text into numbers the model can actually process.

Now here's where it gets interesting.

Those numbers don't just float around independently. Each token gets placed into what's called an **embedding space** — a giant map with hundreds of dimensions where tokens that appear in similar contexts end up near each other.

"King" and "Queen" land close together. "Bank" (financial) and "interest rate" land close together. "Bank" (river) and "current" land close together.

The model learns these neighborhoods entirely from patterns in text — no human drew the map.

[EX]Word2Vec, an early embedding system from Google (2013), famously captured the relationship: King − Man + Woman ≈ Queen. The math worked because those words appeared in similar sentence patterns across millions of documents.[/EX]

[KEY]Embeddings turn token numbers into positions in a meaning-space, where distance reflects how words are used together.[/KEY]

---

[Q]
Why do "bank" (river) and "bank" (finance) get sorted out by the model, even though they're the same token?
A) The tokenizer assigns them different numbers based on context
B) The surrounding tokens shift how the model weighs that token's meaning
C) The model looks up the word in a dictionary during processing
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: can we keep going with the lesson
replies.raw:
Absolutely — and you're doing well so far.

You've got tokenization (text → numbers) and embeddings (numbers → positions in meaning-space). Now for the part that ties it all together.

The model reads your entire sequence of tokens and asks: **which tokens should pay attention to which other tokens?**

This is the attention mechanism. For every token, the model calculates how relevant every other token in the sequence is to understanding it. "Bank" looks left and right — if it sees "fishing rod" nearby, it leans toward the river meaning.

If it sees "interest rate," it leans the other way.

This happens across dozens of layers, each one refining the model's sense of what each token means in context.

[EX]In the sentence "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big," attention lets the model figure out that "it" refers to the trophy — not the suitcase — by weighing which noun the word "big" connects to most strongly.[/EX]

[KEY]Attention lets every token "look at" every other token to figure out what each one means in this specific context.[/KEY]

---

[Q]
What is the attention mechanism's main job?
A) Translating tokens back into readable words
B) Searching the internet for context clues
C) Deciding which tokens are relevant to understanding each other
ANS: C
[/Q]
